In Australia we have public healthcare in a single-buyer system. Basically our government sets the prices to keep things from getting ridiculous and we have various systems in places, things like "bulk billing" and a "pharmaceutical benefits scheme".

Bulk-billing is essentially doctors will see you and you don't pay, the government will pay the cost of seeing a doctor. You also have the option of seeing a private doctor and paying the fee out of pocket, or paying for private medical insurance with co-pay where you pay the difference for your coverage level.

People earning over a certain amount pay a tax if they don't have private insurance, since it's assumed they can afford it. People who cannot afford private medical insurance are allowed on the public system for "free", but they're still paying taxes so they're still essentially paying for government services. People with private insurance have shorter wait-times and more options, whereas people without rely on the public system and services which can become crowded. This system covers everything from general doctors to specialist as well as tests (X-ray, blood-work, etc).

The Pharmaceutical Benefit Scheme is more complicated and I don't really understand it completely, but basically the Australian government sets prices to keep them low while paying the excess to pharma companies that have patents, while also allowing generic versions of the same drug on the market where possible. Typically doctors prescribe the brand-name drug and it's up to the patient to decide if they want the generic when they see their pharmacist.

So basically there is a free system in place paid for out of general taxes and the levy charged to people who can afford private insurance but don't get it, and a private system for people who pay extra. The people with private insurance get better treatment, but people with public aren't left out in the cold. They do have to wait longer, but of course life-threatening situations are given priority.

In the end, when the government pays for the medical treatment for the poor it ends up saving money, since it keeps them in the workforce where they can make money, both by increasing productivity for the nation as a whole, and then said worker contributes even further by having more disposable income because they're working longer hours than they would if they were sick, and that consumption gets taxed when they spend.

And none of this prevents private practice either. There are private doctors who don't "bulk bill" (i.e. see public patients) and private testing services, even entire private hospitals.

I'm not a socialist by any means, but health is one area where I am yet to see a pure capitalist solution work. A system where the government provides a service while also allowing private enterprise to compete with them for those who can afford is, in my opinion, the best of both worlds.

Can't speak for Canada, but it's a trainwreck in Ireland. We're a first world country with an enormous health budget per capita, so there's no excuse. If it could work anywhere, it should work here.

Pretty much all emergency care is public, and the standard of care is bad, so is availability. I keep hearing that the US needs socialised healthcare so the poor can get treatment if they need it, but what this means for us is that the poor get told to get in line and hope they get to the top before they die. The problem is called the "trolley crisis," because even after you get through triage patients get stockpiled in corridors on gurneys for days before seeing someone. I'm not exaggerating, people with serious illnesses have to wait for literally days just to talk to a doctor, not even get treatment. A friend of mine went to hospital with the symptoms of appendicitis and waited 18 hours to be triaged, they told her they didn't know what it was, but symptoms were subsiding so they told her to go home. If it had been appendicitis she'd have been dead before she got seen.

That's just emergency medicine. For anything that isn't an emergency, but still time critical, like cancer treatment, you have to wait to see a consultant. Getting on the list takes months, once you're there, getting an appointment takes years, and the consultant you see might be completely incompetent (I once saw someone about an ENT issue and he wrote a report detailing the exact opposite of the symptoms I described). A friend of mine was on a list for 8 months or so waiting to see an ocular surgeon about a hereditory curable condition. The day before the interview his secretary called to say he wasn't available and had to cancel, she rescheduled it for a couple of months time, by which time her sight was already all but lost.

The other argument is that centralising everything under the government makes it more efficient and less costly to the consumer. This is complete bullshit. There used to be four regional health boards in Ireland, then they amalgamised them all into a single corporation (the HSE). The idea was to cut down on excess bureaucracy and replicated work, but because of public unions raising a stink, they kept everyone on with their original contracts and created a new layer of bureaucrats to oversee it all. I've never seen the exact numbers on how many paper pushers they employ per healthcare worker, but it's way more than 1:1. I've known a couple of people working in similar government quangos and departments, one of them said he played games in excel all day, the other one actually worked, but she was the only one doing so in the office.

Suffice to say, I'm not a fan. Socialism kills.
